text: Hi, everyone.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm Victor.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm a product manager here at LangChain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I primarily focus on our runtime products, and today we're going to talk about deploying mission-critical agents into production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're going to start first with a little refresher on what deep agents are, and then we'll talk about managed deep agents and why we're so excited about them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the first place we always love to start with this is what is an agent?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a question we get a lot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the core idea of an agent is it's a model using tools in order to complete a task.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is based on the React-style agents that have become popular over a year ago.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's based on reason and action.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So they're going to use tools.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're going to reason over it to accomplish a task for you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The next question we often get is what is a harness?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So a harness is basically everything else that we bake in to create the agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that can be skills, it can be tools, context, sub-agents, really all of these different things that we put into an agent in order for it to accomplish a task.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Why do we do this?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Why do we go through all the effort of building a harness, building an agent, and going through all this development?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's to get the model the right context at the right time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So a lot of times when we're building an agent, we know that the model is only as powerful as the context that we give it, and we need to always be able to get it the right context at the right time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Deep Agents is a customizable harness that we can build for any domain-specific task.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we took a lot of the learnings of coding agents and different harnesses that are out there in the wild, and we've really put it into this very customizable base harness that you can use for virtually any use case.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The anatomy of a deep agent is really comprised of four core areas, the first being the execution environment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is really core to the philosophy of deep agents is we sort of abstract away the file system for the agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So us as developers, we can define sort of this wall between your model and the files it interacts with through a virtual file system.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That file system can actually live anywhere.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It could be S3 files.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It could even be a sandbox where your agent can write and execute code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Or its lighter weight cousin, a code interpreter, or a REPL.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What's really cool about this too is this helps with context management.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So things like progressive disclosure of skills, doing things like cross-thread memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you want to remember things about users across threads.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can do that with the file system.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We can do things like summarization.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So as our context grows and grows, we're able to summarize the previous steps of the conversation, compact it down, and store it in the file system.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we can also offload context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's say we retrieve a very large tool response.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We can actually offload that into the file system rather than directly loading that into our model's context window.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The third kind of key area is delegation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So delegation is the ability for the model to plan, reason over that plan, and then kick off sub-agents to execute things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then lastly is human in the loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Human in the loop is very core to everything that we do here at LangChain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This conference is actually named after the interrupt function, which is a function in LangGraph.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: DeepAgent is built on top of that LangGraph runtime, so you have that ability to interrupt and pause for execution.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So a good example of taking a deep agent into production is a customer of ours, which is Madrigal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Madrigal has a ton of different use cases, but primarily focuses on a pharmaceutical research agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is for their pharmaceutical researchers to be able to load in a domain-specific harness that is able to reason over a certain knowledge base for that particular researcher's domain, synthesize all of those results, and respond back with a cohesive report with cited sources and all of that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They were able to build all of this with Deep Agents, and a task that used to take them weeks to spin up a new agent for a researcher now just takes a few hours by putting this all into the Deep Agents harness and deploying it onto LangSmith.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Cool.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's talk about what it takes to take an agent from something that works locally and actually put it into production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So there's kind of like three core areas of building an agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first is the business logic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is what we think is the most important thing for developers and for teams to bring, is this core idea of their expertise and the different instructions and skills that your agent might use.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second is the harness itself, which we talked about as deep agents, gives our agent the ability to use files and do context management and all these wonderful things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the third area is going to be infrastructure.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So infrastructure is probably the more boring area, but the most important area when you talk about actually taking the agent and putting it into production in a way that others can use it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Cool.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So one of the first things that we do when we're building an agent is we're prototyping it locally.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We get it running locally in our machine, and it works great, and we're really excited, and then we want to go and actually share this with everyone else.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is actually a very, very valuable stage.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is where we can kind of prove the magic of the agent, that the agent can actually do what we're designing it for.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What happens then is we try to go into production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And now we need to think about a lot of different things, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We need to think about where people are going to use this agent, the different surfaces you might want your agent to be used from, how you're going to reconcile where those different surfaces are entering into your actual runtime,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You need to be able to queue up the runs so that your agent can kind of serve them reasonably.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You need to be able to establish streaming.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You need to do all these different things in order to have this agent run reliably in production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it requires kind of different things that your team has to consider from an infrastructure standpoint.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: With Manage Deep Agents, we wanted to make this process very, very easy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what we've done is we've sort of bundled together the harness and the infrastructure to make it really, really easy for your teams to work on primarily the business logic and actually improving your agents with evals, with traces, with engine, and iterating on your actual agent logic rather than focusing on the infrastructure and the harness level stuff.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is kind of what it looks like, that previous graph of all these different boxes that you had to manage yourself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now it becomes very easy with Manage Deep Agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It runs on our proven LangSmith deployment for things like streaming, checkpointing, auth handlers, things of that nature.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It integrates directly with LangSmith sandboxes for all of that sandbox control when you need agents to run and execute code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It also uses Context Hub, which we'll talk about a little bit later, but allows us to kind of coordinate on instructions and skills with business users and iterate on things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then of course it plugs into our LLM gateway and traces as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what's really nice is on the left side you'll see this agent interface is we do a really good job of allowing you to use your agent from different interfaces and reconcile those.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So since we're handling all this infrastructure, we now can make it really easy for you as a developer to define the agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So rather than kind of defining it in your own logic, we can go ahead and give you this folder structure in order to define things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So your agent will live in like the agent.ts or agent.py, so this works for Python or TypeScript.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your instructions, skills, tools, identity, all of these different primitives that you need to add to the agent itself will live in different folders or different files in your directory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Getting started is really easy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So all we're going to do is run mda init and give our agent a name.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That'll scaffold this project directory for us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: After we add in all of that logic, we can then go ahead and run MDADev.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's going to start up a local agent server for us, which is the same server that powers LangSmith deployment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you're able to test everything out locally and make sure that it's working as intended.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then once you're ready to actually go into production, all you need to do is run MDADeploy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's going to go ahead and deploy it onto LangSmith's managed infrastructure.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This makes it really, really easy to go from an idea to a prototype, something that works locally, and then into production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Cool.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's take a look at an actual example of an agent that you might want to build and something that people in your organization might use.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is sort of an example that we use a lot internally here at LangChain, which is our go-to-market agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it's something that anyone in our organization can interact with in order to do anything related to go-to-market.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we're going to ask it to prep me for a certain meeting and draft an email for me to review.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that kind of gets sent into this GTM agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The way that this looks and the way that we can design this agent is really quite easy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This now all maps to different files.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So again, our agent definitions at the beginning, the sort of playbook for how we wanted to do different things can live in both the instructions and the skills, and then all of the connections to different business systems like Salesforce, Gong, all these other sort of platforms lives in tools.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we can define how users authenticate and how we remember things about users in the other two files.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So one of the core things that when we talk about building agents with customers, there's kind of four scary things that then get brought up when you bring it into production is how do we identify who's asking this agent to do what, you know, prep for the email or prep for the meeting?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Whose data is it going to use?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Which memory is it going to be able to reference or edit?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then lastly, what happens if it is actually missing access when that run, it gets initiated?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So jumping into the first one, this is something that we thought about a lot with Managed Deep Agents is being able to reconcile the colors between different surface areas.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we have first class support for different channels in Managed Deep Agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can really easily just create a Slack application, go ahead and use this agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But you also might want to expose this agent in your web UI or your web application or your own platform.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you don't want to have to have a user always re-authenticate and go through the permissioning over and over again.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what we did is built a very nice auth handler that will help you reconcile those users, and you can have them reconcile across these different surface areas.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that all gets passed into the runtime for the managed deep agent quite easily.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second is whose account should it use?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So as a developer, we might want to define certain connections, certain tools that your agent can use and connect them in a certain way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we might want to say, okay, when it uses our CRM tool, for example, we always want it to use the user's credentials.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we want to have it operate on behalf of the caller.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So if I'm in a DM with this agent and I say, prep me for this meeting, it's then going to be able to use my Salesforce credentials and go and access that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's other scenarios where you might want your agent to have its own agent scope credentials or be able to have service account credentials.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We make this really easy and manage deep agents with this connections primitive.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So all you need to do is define these connections, upload tokens.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If they're user-based, we'll actually handle that for you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And how we handle that is really easily mid-task.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So since we have built-in Hume in the loop in deep agents and in the LangGraph runtime, what happens is when you make a request and the agent doesn't have a particular token for a particular user, and it's an on behalf of token, it's actually able to really easily pause, ask the user to go ahead and authenticate, they'll click the link, everything proceeds as normal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this will happen indefinitely since we have the interrupts checkpointed.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The third core area that becomes interesting is memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's a lot of different approaches to memory, and we wanted to have really good defaults for this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the first convention is agent-level memory or procedural memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have a really great way for your agent to be able to take and remember certain procedural things about users and manage deep agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second is user-level memory, so personal preferences that I tell the agent about myself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it's really important that your agent is able to take these different types of memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is where control starts to come into place.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So one thing that we built into manage deep agents is allowing you to define the access control based on the channel that it's calling from.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So if I'm in a Slack DM, for example, it can use my personal memories, it can use my personal credentials, it can take personal memories about me, and that's totally fine.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But if I'm talking in a shared channel with my other coworkers, I probably don't want it to be able to unveil certain information about me.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So as a developer, I can define those sort of primitives if I need to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Another really nice part of Manage Deep Agents is we get version control for our agent context with Context Hub.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we're able to store all of our instructions, skills, and memory inside of a Context Hub repo, and that will allow us to collaborate in the surface within LangSmith, which is really great for kind of iterating on different things like instructions, having version control over it, promoting it to production, things of that nature.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Promoting it to production, though, can be scary.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So one thing that we built into Managed Deep Agents that we've really spent a lot of time on was its integration with Harbor as an eval framework.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I know we've talked about Harbor today, but we really think it's a great, great way for running evals.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But what we found from customers is that it can be a bit difficult to get started with.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you run this mda evals init,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It'll go ahead and initialize a harbor environment for you, help you set up the tasks, help you set up the checks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All of that will get traced into LangSmith and show up in your LangSmith experiments tab, and you're able to kind of improve your agent over time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can rerun the same tasks, and you can actually hill climb your agent right in your own machine.
